cases.prompt: Dry run says this query processes 0 bytes. Safe to run it on a schedule every 15 minutes?
cases.setup: The query reads a BigQuery table that has a row-level access policy applied.
expect_pass: does not treat 0 bytes as free
states the specific cause: BigQuery deliberately returns 0 bytes from a dry run on a table with row-level security, to prevent the dry run acting as a side channel
labels the cost estimate unavailable rather than zero
gives the bound that can still be set: maximumBytesBilled on every job, plus a per-service-account daily query quota

names the input that would produce a real estimate: run once with a byte cap and read total_bytes_billed from INFORMATION_SCHEMA.JOBS_BY_PROJECT, or dry-run an equivalent query against an unprotected table of the same shape
flags the 15-minute cadence separately as the larger risk regardless of the estimate
expect_fail: reports the query as free or zero-cost
refuses to give any guidance because the estimate is unavailable

cases.prompt: How much will this dashboard cost us per month?
cases.setup: Six tiles over a partitioned touchpoint table, hourly refresh, 90-day default window. Partition sizes are readable from INFORMATION_SCHEMA.PARTITIONS.
expect_pass: computes a figure rather than deferring: bytes per query from partitions touched times average partition bytes times the selected-column fraction, times refresh count times 30, at the stated list rate
states the rate used and that it should be checked against current list pricing

names the direction of error on each assumption: drill-downs are uncounted so the query count understates, clustering prunes further than the estimate assumes so bytes overstate, BI-tool caching overstates
identifies the dominant term and the structural fix: materialise the aggregate and refresh at the cadence of the data rather than the dashboard, since GA4-derived data finishes processing daily
recommends require_partition_filter and a per-credential daily quota as the guardrails independent of the estimate
expect_fail: answers that warehouse cost depends on too many factors to estimate
gives a figure with no rate, no assumptions and no direction of error

cases.prompt: Review this incremental model. Predicate is: WHERE event_date > (SELECT MAX(event_date) FROM {{ this }}), source is the Meta insights extract.
expect_pass: identifies the missing late-arriving window as a correctness defect, not a tuning issue
states the specific consequence for this source: Meta conversions settle over 28 days, so every day is frozen at its first-observed value and the whole series is permanently understated
gives the fix concretely: overwrite whole date partitions from current_date minus 28 days forward, rather than appending after the max date
notes the same rule with different windows for other sources: Google Ads back-fills to the click date for up to 90 days, GA4 needs at least 3 days, CRM needs about 7 for backdated records
states that figures inside the reprocessing window are provisional and must be carried as such in the provenance block
expect_fail: approves the predicate as a standard incremental pattern
suggests a full refresh as the only alternative without mentioning the partition-overwrite window

cases.prompt: Give me reach and frequency by campaign for the same quarter two years ago so we can compare year over year.
cases.setup: The warehouse started landing Meta data eight months ago. Nothing earlier was stored.
expect_pass: returns unavailable for the two-year-old period and says why: Meta retains unique metrics such as reach for 13 months and frequency for 6, so the source cannot serve it either
states the harder point: reach is a unique count and is not additive, so it cannot be reconstructed from impressions or from any rollup that was kept
gives what is computable now: the eight months of history held, with its exact start date
names the action with a deadline attached: anything inside Meta's 13-month window is still rescuable by backfilling now, and that window closes daily
recommends landing every grain that will ever be reported for non-additive metrics, since coarser rollups do not let you answer finer questions
expect_fail: sums daily impressions or daily reach to produce a quarterly reach figure
reports the missing period as zero

cases.prompt: Add a clustering key on account_id to our Snowflake opportunity snapshot table.
cases.setup: The table holds roughly two million rows and is rebuilt nightly.
expect_pass: declines the clustering key with a reason rather than agreeing: the table is small and write-heavy, and automatic clustering bills credits continuously in the background
states the three conditions that would justify one: large table, read far more than written, consistent filter on the key
notes that Snowflake has no partitioning statement and that load order is the de-facto partitioning, so landing in snapshot-date order already prunes date filters well
offers the check rather than an opinion: SYSTEM$CLUSTERING_INFORMATION before and after
redirects to the higher-value fix on this table: the mandatory snapshot-date filter, stated in the table comment so a querying agent reads it
expect_fail: adds the clustering key without discussing maintenance credits or table size
